title: The gaming console wars just got weird...

segments.text: It's a gaming console. No, it's a Linux
PC. No, it's the new Steam machine. A
black box that lets you harvest organs
on Rim World. Then hit tab to switch
into a Linux desktop where you can hack
into the Pentagon from your couch. For
the first time in history, a gaming
console ships with a package manager.
Instead of Windows Bloatware, you get
Steam OS, a Linux DRO with big picture
mode duct taped on top of it. While
other consoles like Xbox and PlayStation
brag about exclusive titles, this thing
brags about Pac-Man flag SYU. Because
this black box is running Arch Linux
under the hood, and that means finally
every gamer will be able to say, "I use
Arch, by the way." And it's even got a
customizable LED strip, y'all. In
today's video, we'll break down the
details of the brand new Steam Machine
and find out if 2026 will finally be the
year of the Linux desktop. It is
November 14th, 2025, and you're watching
the Code Report. Back [music] in 2015,
Valve's original Steam machine crashed
harder than a Segfold in production on a
Friday deploy. But like a developer who
refuses to accept their PR got rejected,
Valve spent the last decade secretly
building the most based gaming platform
in existence today. And did I mention it
runs Arch Linux, by the way? From an
enduser standpoint, that means you can
be playing AAA games on your television
set at one moment, then quickly switch
into a fullyfledged PC and clock into
your remote job and pretend like you're
doing something productive. What's
especially unique is that this operating
system is not Windows-based like most
gaming PCs, but rather Linux- based
thanks to Steam OS, which have I
mentioned is based on Arch Linux, by the
way, and uses KDE Plasma as the desktop
environment. In addition, you should
know that you're not limited to just
playing Linux native games thanks to
Valve's work on an open- source project
called Proton, which is a compatibility
layer that allows Windows games to run
seamlessly on Linux. But at the same
time, you're also not locked into
playing Steam games only. You can easily
switch over to desktop mode and launch
any game or app store that you want.
Inside the box, it's got a semi-custom
AMD chip that clocks in at 4.8 GHz. It's
got 16 GB of RAM, plus 8 GB of VRAM and
a semi-custom AMD GPU that's capable of
running 4K games at 60fps. These
hardware specs are decent, but not crazy
powerful by any stretch of the
imagination, but it should provide more
than enough horsepower for most games.
For perspective, though, I have trouble
running Microsoft Flight Simulator in VR
mode with my own PC that has 64 GB of
RAM and a GTX 4090. So, this thing may
not be for gamers who want to push
things to their absolute max potential.
However, the one thing we don't know yet
is the price. Although Steam has hinted
that their black box will be affordable
and should cost well under $1,000. If it
cost around five, six, or even $700, it
would be an incredible value. So, when
Trump's $2,000 STEMI checks hit our bank
accounts, it should be easily affordable
for everyone. It sounds awesome, but
there are some drawbacks to the Steam
machine. The hardware is fixed into the
system, which means less upgrade
flexibility than a full desktop PC, and
who knows if it'll be able to run GTA 6
when it finally comes out in 2028. And
if you're a developer, especially an
Arch user who wants full control over
every bit on the system, the Steam OS
flavor of Arch is probably not ideal.
